Artifacts

An artifact is any physical piece of information used or produced by a system. 

In Enterprise Architect these are represented by the Artifact element, which can have one of a number of stereotypes to tailor it to a specific purpose, including internal operations and structures within the model.

Various artifact elements are provided on the toolbox pages 'Documents', 'Charts', 'Governance', Dynamic Viewpoints' and 'Simulation'.  Basic artifacts and Document artifacts are also provided on the 'Deployment' and 'Documentation' toolbox pages.
Document Artifact

A Document Artifact is an element that is used to store an RTF document, directly inside the model repository.

Document Artifacts can be linked to any other element in the model repository.  Within the document itself, you can also insert hyperlinks to other model elements and diagrams.
Double-click on this example Document Artifact, to open its Linked Document in Enterprise Architect's built-in document editor.

The base Artifact element provides a means for connecting elements in the repository with external files or web resources. When a file or resource is dragged onto a diagram, a menu will prompt the user to select the type of Artifact to create:
  • 'Hyperlink' creates a Hyperlink element on the diagram; you can select a sub-option to define what happens when double-clicking on the Hyperlink: 'Open' displays the file content and 'Edit' opens it within the assigned file editor
  • 'External' creates an Artifact element on the diagram that stores a hyperlink to the external file; press F12 or Ctrl+E to open the external file
  • 'Internal' creates an Artifact element on the diagram and makes a copy of the file inside the repository; double-clicking the Artifact launches the internal document
  • 'Insert' (graphics files only) inserts the file into the diagram as a filled Boundary element
You can also create Artifact elements by dragging one of the 'Artifact' icons from various pages of the Diagram Toolbox.
Artifact
Other Artifacts

The tool box pages listed above offer a range of other Artifact types that can be created and placed on a diagram. Double-clicking the Artifact on the diagram will typically open or run the associated specification. They include:
  • Matrix Specification - encapsulates a saved Relationship Matrix profile
  • Report Specification - encapsulates a saved Document Generation specification
  • Model View - represents a table of model data, retrieved using a custom SQL search
  • Standard Chart - an artifact that records information for generating a bar chart or pie chart from data in your model; once you have defined the chart, it automatically displays with the latest information whenever you open the parent diagram
  • Time Series Chart - an artifact that records information for generating a linear graph of model properties over time; once you have defined the chart, it automatically displays with the latest information whenever you open the parent diagram
  • Executable StateMachine - an artifact that specifies the objects that will be involved in a simulation
  • SysMLSim Configuration - records a specific SysML simulation configuration
  • Image Asset - an artifact used to store an image in the model repository
  • Reading List - provides an ordered list of elements; information from each element is displayed in the 'Dynamic Document' view
  • Checklist - facilitates creation of a list of items, each with a checkbox
  • User Story - provides a Linked Document, for recording a Business Use Case
  • Working Set - a saved profile that specifies a workspace layout

Auto Names and Counters

The 'Auto Names and Counters' facility allows you to configure the default name that is generated for specific element types.  A user defined prefix and suffix is combined with a counter value, to create a default name.  For example, 'REQ' + '00268' + ' - '.

When a new element of the specified type is created, its name field is populated with this default.  You can add a brief description to the generated name before saving, so the resulting element name might be 'REQ00268 - Manage User Accounts'.

This feature is particularly useful when dealing with large and complex sets of requirements, as it allows analysts to communicate unambiguously about the requirements without having to use long and cumbersome requirement names.
See also:

To display the 'Auto Name Counters' dialog, from the ribbon, select the option:
'Settings > Reference Data > Settings > Auto Names and Counters'.
Boundary Elements
Stakeholder Onion Diagram

The Boundary element is particularly useful for defining what is inside a system and what is outside. It is derived from the Use Case system boundary, but can be used extensively in other contexts as a way of describing the separation between a system (or part of a system) and its external environment.
Any number of Boundaries can be added to a diagram, with other elements such as Use Cases, Features or Requirements placed inside the boundary.  Boundary elements can also be nested within one another, using different fill colors to show the different levels.
The Boundary can be configured to have a number of vertical and horizontal swimlanes, which are useful for grouping elements into different sections of the boundary.
They can also be set to have a variety of different styles which allow you to customize their shape where required.
Boundary elements can be found on the 'Common' toolbox page.
You can find additional information, including more details of their style options here.
Browser window

To show the Browser window, select the ribbon option:  'Start > All Windows > Design > Explore > Browse'.
The Browser window is the primary tool for structuring and organizing the content of your project repository.
It presents the model as a hierarchical tree structure, consisting of Packages, diagrams and elements.
Packages can contain diagrams, elements and other Packages.  Elements can contain attributes and operations, as well as diagrams and other elements.

The key structural element is the Package, which is a folder-like element that can contain diagrams, elements and other Packages.

With the Browser window, you can easily review the model structure and if required, modify it by simply dragging items from one location to another.  Tree nodes including Packages, diagrams, elements and Features (the attributes and operations of an element) can also be copied and pasted between locations.

Context menus for each of the different node types within the Browser window provide a wide range of commands for working with each of the different node types.

Typically, the Browser window would be docked on one side or the other of your Enterprise Architect workspace, but it can also be 'floated' to any position on your desktop workspace, or hidden altogether.
The image here shows an example of the Browser window, illustrating several levels of nesting of Packages and displaying many of the different types of tree nodes.
Data Flow Diagrams

The Data Flow Diagram (DFD) is part of the Structured Systems Analysis and Design Method.  It is one of the three essential perspectives of Structured Systems Analysis and Design Method SSADM.

DFDs are used to illustrate the way that data flows through a system, showing the Processes, Data Stores and Entities that relate to the data.

With a data flow diagram, users are able to visualize how the system will operate, what the system will accomplish and how the system will be implemented. Developing a DFD helps in identifying the transaction data in the data model.  A data flow diagram can also be used for the visualization of data processing (structured design).

It is common practice for a designer to draw a context-level DFD first, which shows the interaction between the system and outside entities.  This context-level DFD is then "exploded" to show more detail of the system being modeled.'

To create a new Data Flow diagram, from the ribbon select the option:  
'Design > Diagram > Add Diagram > Data Flow Diagrams > Data Flow Diagram'.

This is a Data Flow diagram that shows the way that information (or data) flows through an organization.
The modeler has chosen to use color to make it easier to see the data sources and where the data flows to.
Decision Tables

Enterprise Architect provides support for Decision Tables, based on the OMG Decision Model and Notation (DMN) specification (2014).
DMN is designed to be used alongside BPMN and to support the exchange of decision models across organizations via XML.
The Decision Tables facility provides a simple method of modeling how a decision is made, and provides the capability of generating code for the decisions.  It is possible to generate the method code of a Class from an Activity element, based on the logic defined in its Decision Table, by placing the Activity as a child of the Class element from which the code is generated.
Decision Tables are created as part of an Activity or an Action element.  This is achieved by right-clicking the element then choosing 'Decision Table' from the context menu, or by selecting the element and then choosing the ribbon option:  'Design > Element > Decisions > Find Decision Models'.
The image shown here, depicts the Decision Table Editor window, with the Decision Table for the Activity element 'RiskAssessment' loaded.

This example illustrates how you could model a decision on an insurance Risk Rating, based on the applicant's age and medical history.

Select the class 'Actuary' on this diagram, then press F11 to generate code for the class.
Press F12 to view the source code that was generated.
Element Appearance

Changing the appearance of an element on a diagram, or a selection of elements, can provide a useful visual cue to highlight a particular business meaning.
While all elements in the repository have a global default appearance, the default can be overridden for individual elements either globally or for specific diagrams.  The Fill Color, Border Color, Line Thickness, Font Style and Font Color can all be changed, as global defaults for all elements, as global settings for specific elements, or as local settings for a specific element on a particular diagram.
It is also possible to assign a Shape Script or an alternate image to a stereotype and apply that stereotype to particular elements, as well as assigning an alternate image to a specific element.

To configure the default appearance for all elements, from the 'Start' ribbon, select the option:
'Workspace > Preferences > Standard Colors, Appearance'

To configure the global appearance of a specific element, right-click on the element on a diagram, then choose:  'Appearance | Default Appearance'
To configure the local appearance of a specific diagram object, select the object on a diagram and using the 'Layout' ribbon, select options from the 'Style' panel to set Font Style, Font Color, Fill Color, Line Color or Line Thickness.
These elements illustrate some of the options available for setting element appearance.

elements.notes: Element Browser

The Element Browser provides a view of all the important aspects of an element, including Attributes, Operations, Internal Requirements, Relationships, Constraints, Maintenance Items and more, conveniently collected in a single display.

To show the 'Details' tab of the Inspector window, from the ribbon select:
  • 'Start > All Windows > Design > Explore > Inspect > Element'
Select an element either on the 'Project' tab of the Browser window or on a diagram.
The image here shows the Element Browser window displaying details for the Class element 'Transaction'.

Having the Element Browser open provides an overview of which aspects of the element have been detailed, without the need to open several dialogs to view the details. The Element Browser can be used to view and to edit all the important aspects of an element.  Using the Element Browser's context menu, new items can be added to an element and existing ones deleted, directly from the browser window.
Entity-Relationship Diagrams

Entity Relationship Diagrams in Enterprise Architect are based on Chen's ERD building blocks: Entities (tables) are represented as rectangles, Attributes (columns) are represented as ellipses (joined to their entity) and Relationships between the entities are represented as diamond-shape connectors.

ERD technology in Enterprise Architect assists you in every stage, from building conceptual data models to generating Data Definition Language (DDL) for the target DBMS.

Entity-Relationship Diagrams are available from the category 'Entity Relationship Diagrams'.
Flow Chart Diagram

A Flow Chart is a graphical representation of a sequence of events, helping decision makers understand the relationship between their decisions and a given outcome.  Flow Charts use a range of simple geometric shapes to represent a process, decision, storage or output.
Flow Chart diagrams are available from the 'Strategic Modeling' category.  The associated toolbox offers a range of elements and connectors that specifically target that diagram type.
Gap Analysis

The Gap Analysis Matrix is a specialized Relationship Matrix that is used to record gaps that exist between two versions of some part of an enterprise.  The aim is to highlight the shortfall between the Baseline Architecture and the Target Architecture; that is, items that have been deliberately omitted, accidentally left out, or not yet defined.
In the example presented here, the existing Process Model is compared to the Target Process Model.
To open the Gap Analysis Matrix, from the 'Design' ribbon, select the option: 'Package > Gap Analysis', and select and load the saved profile 'Process Gap'.
This profile compares the processes defined in the two 'model' Packages.
Note that the Gap Analysis window was used to create the linked Feature elements in the Package 'Process Gaps'.

Here, the existing Process Model is compared to the Target Process Model. Two new Feature elements, 'Reward Customer Loyalty' and 'Manage Membership details', were created directly from within the Gap Analysis Matrix.

elements.name: Book Catalogue
elements.notes: The book catalogue is stored in an Oracle database on a corporate server. It is a full list of all books that the company handles. Not all books are currently in stock, and will require JIT ordering when a customer requests an out of stock item.

elements.name: Customer
elements.notes: A customer of the on-line book ordering system. The customer will be required to register and log in before using the system. They must have a connection to the Internet to use the system.

elements.name: Customer Order
elements.notes: The Customer Order from the Sell Books on Line process is an activation event that starts the Manage Customer Order process. The outcome of this process should be a delivered order.

elements.name: Delivered Order
elements.notes: The outcome of the Manage Customer Order process is a successfully delivered customer order.

elements.name: Manage Customer Orders
elements.notes: The Manage Customer Orders process is about fulfilling customer orders in a timely and efficient manner. Orders are made up and dispatched via the preferred shipping method. A customer will log on to the web site and inquire on their order and its status.

elements.name: Note
elements.notes: The business process model lets you model the main business activities. A process may involve multiple departments or divisions of a larger entity. It describes something a business does as part of its normal activity; focusing mainly on the inputs, outputs, goals and key events that drive the process.

elements.name: Order
elements.notes: The Sell Books on Line process results in an order being taken for one or more items. This order is then passed to the Order Management Process for order make-up and shipping.

elements.name: Sell Books On-Line
elements.notes:
The sell books on-line process is aimed at allowing on-line Internet customers to log in and browse a catalogue of books. The book catalogue displays a list of books, publisher information, price, discounts, shipping details and other information of interest to a customer. 
The customer may add their selections to a 'shopping basket', and place their electronic order, including payment details using credit card. The order will be passed onto the order management process for shipping and processing.

elements.name: Ship Order
elements.notes: The goal of the Order Management process is to effectively and quickly process customer orders. Efficient and effective shipping processes result in higher customer satisfaction, resulting in better customer relations and greater chance of repeat orders.

elements.name: Shipping Company
elements.notes: The shipping company is responsible for delivering the customer order. A customer may select from a list of preferred shipping agencies.

elements.name: Shopping Basket
elements.notes: An electronic shopping basket allows the customer to add items to their order as they browse the current catalogue. When the customer is ready to place their order, they may review their basket - remove items if desired, then go on to the electronic payment process.

elements.name: Shopping Basket Item
elements.notes: Shopping basket items are stored for the life of the shopping basket. They may be added or removed from (deleted). If the user decides to purchase their basket, the items currently stored are passed to the final ordering process

elements.name: Take Customer Orders
elements.notes: The goal of the Sell Order On-Line process is to supplement the traditional book sales channels. Direct sales to customers with low overhead allow the company to deal in a higher volume market without the traditional outlays associated with stocking retail outlets.

elements.name: User Enquiry
elements.notes: The business process starts when a customer logs into the system and enquires on what books are available.

elements.name: Warehouse Inventory
elements.notes: Book stocks are recorded in the Warehouse Inventory. this includes book ID, quantity, amount on order, amount outstanding and related information.

elements.name: Web Pages
elements.notes: The on-line book ordering system is a web based system. Web pages are built in Microsoft ASP format,  with some additional dynamic effects using XSL style sheets applied to XML. Web pages are stored on a central Windows 2003 server.
Glossary

The Project Glossary is a lexicon of your project's important terms and their meanings, categorized by type.
It allows you to review the technical and business terms already defined for a model, add to the list, delete or change items and filter the list by excluding items of specific types.

You can also define markup styles to be applied to terms of specific types when they are used in generated document reports.

Any number of terms, their types and meanings can be defined and these can be referenced from the notes of model elements. The terms can be included in documentation or generated as a stand-alone report.

When working with domain specific requirement specifications or architectures, it is essential that new terms and over-ridden meanings for common phrases are recorded in a Glossary, to ensure proper understanding of documentation and specifications.

A Glossary Report can be generated as a stand alone report or the Glossary can be included as a section of another document.

The Glossary has a number of options to determine which terms are displayed in the list and to define the style that is used in documentation, for terms of particular types.

To open the Glossary View, from the 'Publish' ribbon, select the option:
'Documentation > Glossary > Glossary View'.

Hand Drawn and Whiteboard Mode are display options available for any diagram, that changes a system-drawn diagram to appear as though it was drawn by hand and, optionally, hand drawn on a whiteboard. 

It is a helpful option for engaging an audience by presenting the diagram in a rough and more immediate style, giving the impression that it is just a sketch that can be changed.

'Layout > Diagram > Appearance > Hand Drawn Mode  or  White Board Mode'.

The Image Manager's main use is to define pictures that can be used as alternative representations for elements in diagrams.

For many business and networking diagrams, when the default appearance of an element, such as a UML Class or Component, is replaced with an image from the Image Manager, the diagram is much more readily understood by its audience.

Enterprise Architect provides a facility for importing from and exporting to CSV files.

The facility can be accessed by selecting the ribbon option:
'Publish > Model Exchange > CSV'.

The import and export facility is completely configurable, via a user defined specification, that is used to map fields in the CSV file to elements and their properties within Enterprise Architect.

Typically, this facility is used to import Requirements that have been recorded using a Spreadsheet or a table in a word processor, however any type of element can be imported in this manner.

Once imported into Enterprise Architect, these elements can then be expanded, refined and linked to other elements, just as you would with any element created within Enterprise Architect.

Similarly, Requirements (and other element types) can be exported from Enterprise Architect to CSV files, for supply to third parties who might request CSV files, or for some type of numerical or statistical analysis.

The Info View is an alternative representation for an element that is typically more appealing to managers or non-technical stakeholders. The Info View displays the name, stereotype, notes and a small icon that represents the type of the element.  It is useful in situations where the audience does not need to know about Attributes, Operations and other details.  The display of other element properties can be configured using the Info View - Visible Properties window.

A portion of the notes will be displayed using the available space in the Info View; if all the notes need to be displayed the diagram element can be resized to provide space for the text.


To enable the Info View, right-click an element on a diagram, then from the element context menu choose:  'Info View | Enabled'.

Model Mail

Most initiatives are carried out by a team of people, and critical to their success is good communication. Model Mail is a mail system internal to the Enterprise Architect repository that allows users to send and receive mail messages.  One of the important advantages that Model Mail provides, is the ability to embed hyperlinks to model elements, allowing the recipient to click through to diagrams, elements, Packages and reviews that are the subject of the mail.
A typical scenario might see one team member sending a message containing a hyperlink to a set of Requirements, asking other team members for their comments.
Model Mail provides options for inserting hyperlinks to a variety of repository items including: Diagrams, Matrices, Images, Searches, Help Topics, Attributes, Operations and Team Reviews.
Model Mail can be accessed from the 'Start' ribbon by selecting the option:  'Collaborate > Mail'.

The Model Search facility can be used to find anything that exists in the repository, locating information easily no matter where it is in the model.
The facility includes a wide range of built-in searches and users can also define their own searches using the Query Builder or SQL Builder.
Objects can be located by searching for the name of an element, text in element notes, a Tagged Value or by searching for specific properties such as when an element was created or who created it.
The result set can be sorted, individual elements can be located in the Browser window.
Search queries can also be saved and used as input for other tools, such as Model Views and the Document Generator.

The Model Search facility can be accessed from any ribbon, by selecting the option:

Model Views

The Model Views facility allows the modeler to create a number of views that can be used to group elements and diagrams in whatever combination the modeler requires.
There are options to create 'Favorites' folders, 'Slide-Show' folders and Search-based folders.
The 'Favorites' folder is useful to keep track of hand picked elements and diagrams of interest. Elements, diagrams and Packages are simply dragged from the Browser window and dropped into a 'Favorites' folder.
The 'Slide Show' folder is useful to create a diagram slide show for the purposes of demonstrating diagrams to a group of people in a workshop or meeting.  In this case, diagrams are dragged from the Browser window and dropped into the 'Slide Show' folder.  The order of the diagrams in the folder determines the order in which they are displayed in the slide show.
The 'Search' folder is useful to keep track of elements that meet specified criteria and to be notified when new elements are added to the Repository that meet the criteria. In the folder properties, you can define the search to be run that populates the folder, and the time period after which the search is re-run to refresh the contents of the folder.
Model views can be created for a variety of purposes and an experienced modeler will often use the Model Views facility as the access point to the Repository.

The effective management of requirements is critical to the success of any project. The properties of Requirement elements allow us to make use of a range of tools in Enterprise Architect that help you to manage those requirements. All Enterprise Architect elements have a number of standard properties including Status, Author and Phase. The Requirement element has two additional properties, Priority and Difficulty. Some requirement processes might specify particular properties that are not part of the standard list, such as Owner and Volatility (Stability); these can be applied using Tagged Values that can be set for each Requirement element. In managing requirements, you could make use of the Model Search facility to retrieve high priority requirements and define work packages for the implementation teams, or you might retrieve requirements for a particular phase of the project. Search results can be used as input for report generation, so you could generate a report on all requirements that are 'owned' by a particular stakeholder. Filters can be employed with diagrams and element lists, allowing you to hide or to highlight requirements that meet specific criteria. Stereotyping

This diagram shows a number of stakeholders and their needs (requirements).
A stereotype has been created for the stakeholders, that has an alternate image assigned to it.
The requirements are displayed using a rectangular presentation style, so as to display the stereotype <<stakeholder requirement>> in the diagram.

Stereotypes are an extension mechanism of the Unified Modeling Language, that can be used to create a new element type based on an existing UML element type.  

There are many cases where defining a new type to model a thing of interest in a particular industry or domain, can be very beneficial.  Stereotyped elements often add clarity to a model, by making the elements more meaningful and recognizable to the audience.  The use of images and shapes can also make the resulting models more readily understood by the audience.  
Examples of stereotypes include a 'contract' stereotype in the legal profession, a 'meter' stereotype in the energy distribution industry or a 'stakeholder requirement' in the business analysis profession.

Care should be taken not to overuse the facility as it can lead to fragmentation of meaning and can also result in models that are not easily understood by external audiences.

To define new Stereotypes, from the ribbon, select the option:
'Settings > Reference Data > UML Types > Stereotypes'.

To apply an existing Stereotype to a model element, open the Properties window for the element and specify a value in the 'Stereotype' field.
Tagged Values

Tagged Values are a built-in extension mechanism of the Unified Modeling Language.  They provide a useful and productive way of adding extra properties to elements, attributes, operations or connectors.  Tagged Values consist of:  a Tag name, a Value and additional Notes.

For example, a Requirement element does not have a built in property for Volatility, so a Tagged Value could be added, providing the user with a drop down list of available values: such as High, Low, Medium.

There are built in Structured Tagged Value Types that help the user when entering the value for a tag. The values can be restricted using user interface controls such as drop down lists, spin controls, date selectors and many more.

Tagged Values are used extensively in profiles and technologies. For example, you will use them when working in the BPMN Technology to set properties of Activities or in the Wire Framing Technology to show or hide phone menu buttons and notification bars.

Tagged Values are accessible through the 'Tags' tab on the 'General' page of an element's Properties Sheet, or through the 'Tagged Values' window, which can be opened from the 'Start' ribbon, by selecting the option:  'Windows > Tagged Values'.
Visual Filters
Dynamic Visual Filters
Context Filtering

Visual Filters provide a mechanism for filtering out parts of a diagram or list of elements, based on the values of selected properties.  Filters can be defined for elements or connectors and there are a wide range of criteria that can be set.  By using filters, you can modify the display of diagrams, dimming, hiding or even selecting components that meet specific criteria,  thereby highlighting certain aspects of the diagram, without affecting the structure and integrity of your model. 

Project stakeholders typically have different interests and often only part of a diagram or element list will be relevant to them. Visual filters allow you to present a single diagram in many different ways, by highlighting the elements and connectors that are of interest to specific target audiences.

Filters are stored as part of the model, so a filter you create is available to other users of the model; however, use of a filter is specific to the user, so your use of a filter does not affect another user's view of the diagram.

To access the Filters & Layers window, from the 'Layout' ribbon, select the option:  'Tools > Filters and Layers'.  
This image shows an example of the Filters & Layers window.

The selected element, as well as those directly connected to it, will remain unchanged, while all other elements will be grayed out.
Also, press and hold the L key, this will highlight incoming and outgoing relationships for the selected element.

elements.notes: Domain Model

The Domain Model is a useful mechanism for recording and defining business terms that are identified during Requirements analysis.  It provides a single definition of the terms and their relationships that can be referenced from anywhere within the model.
One of the advantages of using a Domain model is that the terms are modeled as Class elements, which can be linked to other elements within the Domain model itself or to elements in other parts of the model.  They can be used on any number of diagrams, and they can be displayed as a list, using the Package List window.
It is also possible to create hyperlinks within the Notes text of Requirement elements that link directly to relevant Domain elements.

elements.name: Take Customer Orders

elements.name: User

elements.name: Eligibility

elements.name: Post-bureau affordability
elements.notes: The Post-bureau affordability decision logic invokes the Affordability calculation business knowledge model, passing Applicant data.Monthly.Income as the Monthly Income parameter, Applicant data.Monthly.Repayments as the Monthly Repayments parameter, Applicant data.Monthly.Expenses as the Monthly Expenses parameter, the output of the Post-bureau risk category decision as the Risk Category parameter, and the output of the Required monthly installment decision as the Required Monthly Installment parameter.

elements.name: Post-bureau risk category

elements.name: Pre-bureau affordability

elements.name: Pre-bureau risk category
elements.notes: The Pre-Bureau Risk Category decision logic invokes the Pre-bureau risk category table business knowledge model, passing Applicant data.ExistingCustomer as the Existing Customer parameter and the output of the Application risk score decision as the Application Risk Score parameter.

elements.name: Required monthly installment
elements.notes: The Required monthly installment decision logic invokes the Installment calculation business knowledge model, passing Requested product.ProductType as the Product Type parameter, Requested product.Rate as the Rate parameter, Requested product.Term as the Term parameter, and Requested product.Amount as the Amount parameter.

elements.name: Routing

Requirements Modeling

Enterprise Architect provides a range of facilities for capturing and managing Requirements as UML elements, directly in the model.  In doing so, Enterprise Architect integrates Requirements Management with other software development disciplines.
Representing a requirement as a UML element helps you to trace requirements to other UML elements such as other requirements, use cases, test cases, and analysis or design elements. This element can be used to model or document any requirements ranging from formal business requirements through to performance or security requirements.

Requirements Checklists

Enterprise Architect offers a 'Requirements Checklist' artifact as one of the element types that can be created on a diagram.  

The 'Requirements Checklist' can be associated with any Requirement element, so that Analysts and Requirements Managers can use the checklist to annotate whether a Requirement meets a set of predefined checks.  The list of items is completely configurable:  double-clicking the Checklist element opens a list editor.

The Requirements Checklist is derived from and operates in the same way as an ordinary Checklist artifact, but it has a predefined list of items that represent 'best practice' qualities for a requirement.  

'Requirements Checklist' artifacts can be found in the Requirements diagram toolbox under 'Extended Requirements'.

Data Modeling

Enterprise Architect provides extensive support for the data modeling discipline, ranging from the representation of information in a conceptual model right down to the generation of database objects. 

Enterprise Architect enables you  to model information at the conceptual, logical and physical layers.  Using a number of standard features, these models can be interconnected, providing traceability. The logical and physical models can also be generated automatically using a fully customizable Transformation engine.
The Database Builder

The Database Builder is a tailored interface, designed to allow all database-related modeling tasks to be performed from a single location.  The interface and its related screens, include only the information relevant to data modeling, thereby streamlining and simplifying the modeling process.

Database Builder

The Database Builder can be accessed from the ribbon, by selecting the option:  'Develop > Data Modeling > Database Builder'.
This image shows the Database Builder loaded with the 'Orders (postgres)' data model as it appears in the Example model.

The Database Builder's interface and its related screens, include only the information relevant to data modeling, thereby streamlining and simplifying the modeling process.  It provides a tailored interface, designed to allow all database-related modeling tasks to be performed from a single location.

The interface of the Database Builder consists of:
  • A Tree of data models, listing all defined data models in the current repository
  • A 'Columns' tab through which you directly manage the Table columns
  • A 'Constraints/Indexes' tab for the direct management of Table constraints such as Primary Keys, Foreign Keys and Indexes
  • An SQL Scratch Pad that you can use to run ad-hoc SQL queries against a live database
  • A 'Database Compare' tab that displays the results of comparisons between the data model and a live database
  • An 'Execute DDL' tab on which you can execute generated DDL against a live database, instantly
You can use the Database Builder to:
  • Create, edit and delete database objects (Tables, Views, Procedures, Sequences and Functions)
  • Create, edit and delete Table constraints (Primary Keys, Indexes, Unique Constraints, Check Constraints and Triggers)
  • Create, edit and delete Table Foreign Keys
  • Reverse engineer database schema information
  • Generate DDL from a modeled database
  • Compare a live database schema with a modeled database
  • Execute generated DDL against a live database
  • Execute adhoc SQL statements against a live database
Physical Data Model

With the aid of a UML profile for data modeling, a physical database schema can be modeled as a Class diagram.
A variety of Database objects can be modeled including tables, foreign keys, views and stored procedures.
Data Definition Language can then be generated directly from the model for a large number of supported database systems.
See also:
All of the elements on this diagram were generated from the platform independent Abstract Class Model, using an MDA Transform.

A Conceptual data model is the most abstract form of data model. It is helpful for communicating ideas to a wide range of stakeholders because of its simplicity.

Note: Platform-specific information, such as data types, sequences, procedures, triggers are all omitted from a Conceptual data model.

In this example of a Conceptual data model, the elements are defined as UML classes and the connectors are depicted using the 'Information Engineering' notation.  The diagram is rendered with the 'hand drawn' setting to give it an authentic concept look.  

Alternatively  the elements could be defined in Entity Relationship notation. Which notation should be use will depend on the experience and preferences of the stakeholders.
Conceptual Data Model
Logical Data Model

Logical Data Models help to define the detailed structure of the data elements in a system and the relationships between data elements. They refine the data elements introduced by a Conceptual Data Model and form the basis of the Physical Data Model. In Enterprise Architect, a Logical Data Model is typically represented using the UML Class notation.

Physical Data Model

The Physical Database Schema can be generated from the Logical Data Model, using EA's built in model transformations.  This provides a useful 'first draft' of the Physical model, from which point detailed data types can be specified, along with indexes and other Database objects, such as Views, Stored Procedures and Triggers.

A physical database schema is modeled as a Class diagram, by using a UML profile for data modeling.
The various Database objects including tables, views and stored procedures are then modeled using UML constructs.
A large number of database systems are supported and Data Definition Language can be generated directly from the model.

Architectural Frameworks

Enterprise Architect offers support for a number Architectural Frameworks, including ArchiMate, TOGAF and Zachman Framework.

There are UML Profiles for each of these frameworks, providing various diagram types with associated diagram toolboxes, providing stereotyped elements and connectors to support the concepts that are modeled in each system.
Zachman Framework

The Zachman Framework is a widely used approach for engineering Enterprise Architecture. The Framework is a simple, logical structure that helps in organizing the information infrastructure of the Enterprise.
The Zachman Framework provides a model-based framework for planning, designing and implementing the Architecture for an Enterprise. The starter model provided with the Add-In, acts as a base upon which you can build the Enterprise Architecture. You can create the appropriate diagrams from the extended Enterprise Architect UML diagram set, using Toolbox pages that support every cell of the Zachman classification framework.
TOGAF

The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF) is one of the most widely accepted methods for developing Enterprise Architecture, providing a practical, definitive and proven step-by-step method for developing and maintaining Enterprise Architecture.

TOGAF embodies the concept of the Enterprise Continuum to reflect different levels of abstraction in an architecture development process.  It provides a context for the use of multiple frameworks, models, and architecture assets in conjunction with the TOGAF ADM.  By means of the Enterprise Continuum, architects are encouraged to leverage all other relevant architectural resources and assets, in addition to the TOGAF Foundation Architecture, in developing an organization-specific IT architecture.
ArchiMate

ArchiMate® is an open-standard, enterprise architecture language from The Open Group, based on the IEEE 42010 standard. It offers a common language for describing the construction and operation of business processes, organizational structures, information flows, IT systems and technical infrastructure, that can be used by Enterprise Architects to describe, analyze and clearly visualize, the relationships between business domains.
A number of examples from The Open Group's 'ArchiMate ® 3.0 Specification' have been replicated here, to illustrate how ArchiMate 3 can be used to model your Enterprise Architecture.
The diagrams for these examples can be accessed using the buttons described here.

The Non-Functional Requirements Package specifies the various operational parameters that define the environment in which the system will exist. These are criteria that define performance levels, scalability, security requirements, backup, disaster recovery and other operational requirements.

The Functional Requirements package details behavioral requirements that specify how a proposed system will process and handle information. It details the features and rules that must be present to fully implement the functionality desired.

elements.name: Note
elements.notes:
The Requirements model is a structured catalogue of end-user requirements. These are represented as either Requirement or Feature elements.

The model is divided into two sub-catalogues:

1. The Functional requirements package contains requirements and features that represent functional behavior and features that the system under development must support.

2. The Non-functional requirements package contains constraints and performance levels the system must meet. For example response times, transactions per second, security strength.

elements.name: Note
elements.notes: Functional Requirements describe the features, behavior, business rules and general functionality that the proposed system must support.

elements.name: Note
elements.notes: These packages contain non-functional requirements specified for the new system. These typically describe performance criteria, reliability, security and other operational parameters.

elements.notes: Designer Perspective - People (Who)

This package contains use cases which define how an Actor will interact with the proposed system. 

Each interaction may be specified using scenarios, sequence diagrams, communication diagrams and other dynamic diagrams or textual descriptions which together show the system when viewed as a "black-box" interacts with a user.

Actors are the users of the system being modeled. Each Actor will have a well-defined role, and in the context of that role have useful interactions with the system.

A person may perform the role of more than one Actor, although they will only assume one role during one Use Case interaction.

An Actor role may be performed by a non-human system, such as another computer program.

elements.name: Note
elements.notes:
The Use Case model is a catalogue of system functionality described using UML Use Cases. Each Use Case represents a single, repeatable interaction that a user or "actor" experiences when using the system. 

A Use Case typically includes one or more "scenarios" which describe the interactions that go on between the Actor and the System, and documents the results and exceptions that occur from the user's perspective.

Use Cases may include other Use Cases as part of a larger pattern of interaction and may also be extended by other use cases to handle exceptional conditions

Business Capability Analysis

By modeling and analyzing Business Capabilities, we can assess how well an organization is performing, in its efforts to achieve its business goals and objectives.
As part of its support for Business Architecture, Enterprise Architect offers a variety of tools that can assist in analyzing Business Capabilities.
Relationship Matrix
Roadmap Diagram
Class Diagram
Browser window
Stereotyping
Visual Filters

The Relationship Matrix can be used to provide a clear view of how the business capabilities are meeting both current and future objectives. Once the Business Capabilities have been defined in the model, they can be related to a range of different element sets including Use Cases, Functional Requirements and Business Processes. Overlays can be added to the matrix cells expressing things like the degree of compliance, effectively adding another dimension to the matrix. Matrix Specification artifacts can be saved in the model, allowing you to define any number of matrices that can be easily re-opened in the future.

A Roadmap diagram can be used to show how Capabilities change over time and to represent phases in the lifecycle of the Capabilities. The diagram has a Legend that is integrated with the elements on the diagram and can be used to express concepts such as Capability Definition, Acquisition, Support and Retirement. Colors can be assigned to the dimensions defined in the Legend and the time scale of the diagrams can be configured to suit the time scale of the Capability model.

Capabilities can be modeled using a Stereotyped UML Class element.  Stereotyping enables the creation of a type that represents a Business Capability.  These can be added to a Class Diagram and connected by aggregation relationships to show a tree of Capabilities down to any level.  The Capabilities can also have connections to a number of other elements including Goals, Objectives Applications and more.

A Business Capability Hierarchy can be created directly in the Browser window without the need to create a diagram. A UML Class is a good way to capture the Business Capabilities of an organization and these can be created directly in the Browser window. Additional Capabilities can be added under each first level Capability creating a second level. These second level Capabilities can have Capabilities nested under them creating a third level. The resulting tree of Capabilities provides a useful way of describing Functional Decomposition that can be presented to and reviewed by stakeholders.

A Business Capability is not defined as an element type in any of the built-in Toolbox palettes but can be created as a type using the Unified Modeling Language (UML) extension mechanism of Stereotype. The defined Stereotype can then be applied to a Class to create any number of Capabilities that can be added to the model.

Visual Filters can be used to hide or dim parts of the diagram so that other parts can be emphasized. This is particularly useful when presenting a Capability Model Class Diagram to a team in a meeting or demonstration. Context Filtering is easy to setup and will emphasize the currently selected diagram element and its directly connected elements.

To open the Filters & Layers window, select the ribbon option:
'Layout > Tools > Filters and Layers'.
Business Capabilities

The Domain Model (or Business Object Model) is a useful mechanism for describing the important terms of the business. It provides a single definition of the terms and their relationships, that is accessible to all project staff. elements.notes: Roadmap Diagram

The Roadmap Diagram is an overlay that can be applied to any diagram and describes significant phases in elements and how they change with the passage of time.  This is useful for visualizing how a system changes over time, or representing just about any time based data.

Roadmap Diagrams use a dedicated notation, where each element is depicted as a bar divided into colored segments.  Each segment represent a different state of that element.  The states available, the order in which they appear and the colors used are controlled by a Diagram Legend.  The length of each segment of an element then represents the Duration of each state.  Individual segments may be hidden on any given element.

To apply the Roadmap Diagram overlay, choose 'Roadmap Options' from the diagram context menu.

MDG Technology for ArcGIS

ArcGIS via Enterprise Architect provides support for the design of geodatabases for the ArcGIS suite of tools developed by Esri Inc.  A key component of the technology is the UML Profile for ArcGIS.
Once you have modeled an ArcGIS schema in Enterprise Architect, you can export the model to ArcGIS as an XML Workspace document. You can also visualize an existing ArcGIS geodatabase schema, by importing the ArcGIS XML Workspace document into Enterprise Architect.
Workspaces are the folders that contain geodatabases and other files.  They are modeled in Enterprise Architect using a Package stereotyped as «ArcGIS», containing nested packages that model Spatial References, Features and other geospatial concepts.
Click on this button to view an example of an ArcGIS Workspace.

Create your ArcGIS UML model by dropping elements from the ArcGIS Toolbox pages onto an ArcGIS diagram such as this. The 'Features' Package contains your Feature Classes, while the 'Domains' Package contains your Coded Value Domains and Range Domains. Before exporting your model to an ArcGIS schema, you must define at least one Spatial Reference element. Spatial Reference elements are referred to by other schema elements via a dynamically linked Tagged Value, named 'SpatialReference'. A sample Spatial Reference element has been created for you under the 'Spatial References' Package. To add a valid coordinate system and default values to the element, simply select the element 'MySpatialReference' in the Browser window or on a diagram and then from the 'Publish' ribbon, select the option: 'Technologies > ArcGIS > Set Coordinate System'. To export your model as an ArcGIS schema, select the ArcGIS Workspace in the Browser window, then right-click and choose: 'Specialize > Technologies > ArcGIS > Export to ArcGIS Workspace XML'

MDG Technology for GML

Sparx Systems provides an implementation of the Open Geospatial Consortium's Geography Markup Language (GML) 3.3 as an XML grammar for geographical feature modeling capabilities within Enterprise Architect. You can:
  • Apply a UML Profile for the Geography Markup Language (GML) 3.3
  • Make use of customized diagram types and toolbox pages, for convenient access to elements and relationships to model geographical features effectively
  • Generate GML Application Schema files

Stereotyped Classes are used to model concepts in the Geographic Markup Language (GML).
Feature types represent entities in the physical world and Country Codes are modeled using  a Code List.
The model can be generated to create a GML Application Schema using the Forward Engineering capabilities.

The contents of an «ApplicationSchema» package will be exported as a GML Application Schema file. The tags xmlns, targetNamespace and xsdDocument are mandatory for an «ApplicationSchema» package You can fill in these tags either using:
  • Tagged Values window ( menu: View -> Tagged Values ) ( or )
  • Generate GML Application Schema dialog ( menu: Extensions -> GML -> Generate GML Application Schema )
To generate a GML Application Schema:
  • Select the «ApplicationSchema» Package in the Browser window
  • From the 'Publish' ribbon, select the option: 'Extensions -> GML -> Generate GML Application Schema'

Relationship Matrix

The Relationship Matrix is a spreadsheet display of relationships between model elements within a Package or between elements in two different Packages.
The matrix shows all the relationships of a specified type between source and target elements.  It lists the Source Package elements down the side of the matrix and the Target Package elements across the top of the matrix.  A relationship between two elements is indicated by an arrow where the relevant row and columns intersect, pointing in the direction of the relationship.
The Relationship Matrix can be accessed from the 'Design' ribbon by choosing the option:  <font color="#00008b">'Package > Package/Matrix'</font>.

To see an example of a Relationship Matrix, once open, load the saved profile 'Requirements Trace'.

Enterprise Architect allows modelers to record a range of information associated with model elements, to assist Project Managers in managing the project.  Information such as the Effort required to complete work on an element, the Resources allocated to work on an element, Risks associated with an element, and properties such as the Status of the element.
There is a broad range of facilities available for viewing and updating the various Project Management information items.
Enterprise Architect also provides a message post and reply facility that allows teams to discuss issues relating to an element, such as design decisions or risk mitigation strategies, with the discussion thread being saved as part of the element information.
Click on these buttons to see examples of how to use the various Project Management tools available in Enterprise Architect.
