MDG Technologies
See also:

An MDG Technology is a vehicle for providing access to the resources of either a commercially-available technology or a technology that you have created yourself. 

Anyone can use Enterprise Architect's SDK to create new MDG Technologies.  Using Enterprise Architect, you can develop Stereotypes, Profiles and Design Patterns to build your own customized modeling languages and solutions.  Once the profiles are complete, they can be bundled into an MDG Technology and then used locally within your organization or distributed across entire industries.  

When you create an MDG Technology file, you can include a wide range of facilities and tools, including UML Profiles, Patterns, Tagged Value types, Custom Diagram types and Toolbox pages.  Building all of these into the MDG Technology file in a logical sequence is easy using the MDG Technology Creation Wizard.

Use the link to open the Example UML Profile, then export each of the profiles to XML before using the MDG Technology wizard to bundle them into your own MDG Technology.

Finally, import the Technology into your model, then use it to create your own sample model with customized element and connector types.
Model Exchange
Enterprise Architect provides a number of facilities for exchanging part or all of a model with other tools or with other EA projects.
Reusable Assets Service

Reusable Assets are held in a remote registry, accessed through a Cloud connection. The registry contains any number of Storages, which can either be left unprotected for any user to create, or change-restricted by an Administrator password. Each Storage can contain any number of Asset Packages holding modeling structures, and files containing textual or graphical information and data. When a user creates a Storage, they can protect the contents from being updated in the Registry or downloaded into a model, using password protection defined by that user. Reusable Assets consist of:
  • Packages containing elements, diagrams and structures (as drawn from any point within the Browser window), and
  • Files in a range of text, code and graphic formats, including .eap files
An asset can be, for example:
  • A common Class library or framework
  • A set of common Requirements or Use Cases
  • A draft specification document
  • Marketing collateral
The RAS gives distributed teams convenient access to a single 'source of truth' for shared data, including project milestones, architectural frameworks and industry standards.
See also:

These images illustrate the 'Reusable Asset Service' dialog and the 'Cloud Connection' dialog as they appear when connecting to the Sparx Systems Pro Cloud Server, to install the Enterprise Architect User Guide as a Learning Center Library.
XMI Import and Export

A 'Controlled Package' is a Package configured to save and load in XML format to a named file. Controlled Packages appear in the Browser Window with a small red rectangle to the left of the Package icon. The Package 'Source Pkg' is configured for Package Control. Select the Package on this diagram, then press Alt+G to find the Package in the Browser window. Notice the red rectangle in the Browser window, indicating a 'Controlled Package'. Click the Package in the Browser window, then choose the 'Publish > Model Exchange > Package Control > Package Control' ribbon option to display the 'Package Control Options' dialog. The field 'XMI Filename' specifies the path to the file that is used to 'control' the Package. (Path substitution can be used here, to facilitate the use of different file paths on different users' PCs.) Once a Package is configured as a 'Controlled Package', pressing Ctrl+S will save the Package to its associated XMI file and pressing 'Ctrl+L' will load the Package from the file. Batch Export or Import can also be used to Export or Import a selection of all of the model's controlled Packages in one operation. This can be accessed by selecting the ribbon option: 'Publish > Model Exchange > Export XML > Batch Export Controlled Packages' or 'Publish > Model Exchange > Import XML > Batch Import Controlled Packages'
Controlled Packages
Export to XMI
Import from XMI

Packages can be exported from the model to an XML file, by clicking on the Package in the Browser window and choosing the ribbon option:
'Publish > Model Exchange > Export-XML > Export XML for Current Package'.

Packages can be imported into a model, from an XMI file, by clicking on the intended parent Package in the Browser window, then choosing the ribbon option:
'Publish > Model Exchange > Import XML | Import Package from XML'.
Dashboard Diagrams

The Dashboard diagram toolbox allows high quality charts and graphs to be created, that display project information in a simple and appealing way, providing valuable summary information in a readily consumable format.

The toolbox provides a page of pre-configured charts and graphs, but the user is also free to create and save any number of charts that source data from anywhere in the project.

Charts and Graphs can be placed onto any type of diagram by firstly selecting the Dashboard diagram toolbox, then dragging the desired chart type onto the diagram.  However, the Dashboard diagram toolbox is automatically displayed whenever you open a Dashboard diagram.
The buttons below link to a variety of different charts and graphs.
Heat Maps

A Heat Map is a chart that uses a grid-based layout, where the color, size and grouping of its cells, represent specific aspects of a data set.  Heat Maps are typically used to illustrate co-dependant properties that could influence strategic or project level decisions.

Enterprise Architect supports a number of ways of the retrieving data used to create Heat Maps.  In the examples presented here, the data is defined using CSV lists.

To view the data source for a chart, open its Properties window.

elements.name: Description
elements.notes:
DynamicChart artifacts are Chart elements that are styled and rendered dynamically when the diagram opens. They rely completely on code to define their series, style and content and are managed entirely through the Automation Interface by clients - typically scripts or plug-ins. JavaScript is the primary language used to define Dynamic Charts, but it is also possible to call functions written in other languages. This Package contains examples of many charts, each described dynamically by JavaScript clients. Each chart example presents the two methods of rendering - a JavaScript coding method and a JSON datasource method. Each DynamicChart artifact has a user defined JavaScript function, ConstructChart( ), that is automatically invoked whenever a diagram containing the artifact is opened. That function is responsible for defining the style and populating the data for the chart that is displayed. Using a JSON data source involves two fundamental steps:
  • first, create a JSON variable that defines the styles and data of the chart to render,
  • then call the built-in function ConstructChartFromJSON, passing 'elemGUID' as the first parameter and the JSON structure as the second argument.

Enterprise Architect's Schema Composer streamlines the process of converting model information into standards compliant schemas.  This approach significantly reduces the time taken to form a valid schema and eliminates human error in transcribing model information into schema text.
Modeling Schemas
Schema Composer

Enterprise Architect offers UML Profiles comprising toolboxes that contain stereotyped classes and connectors specific to a number of different schema types. Enterprise Architect offers tools to
  • directly model a schema, building it from scratch,
  • apply model transforms, where a schema model can be generated from a conceptual class model,
  • import an existing schema model that was created using some other tool.
Geospatial Modeling
Schema Modeling

Enterprise Architect offers a number of tools that support creation of schema models for a variety of different domains.
The Schema Composer along with UML Profiles, Toolboxes, Model Patterns and MDG Technologies all provide assistance in creating models for XSD, NIEM, WSDL, ArcGIS, GML and more.

NOTE:  The NIEM 4 Reference Model has NOT been included in the EAExample model due to its very large size.
However, the NIEM MPD Types package, the NIEM 4 Starter Model pattern and the Personalized Message example are included, for your perusal.

National Information Exchange Model (NIEM) provides a common framework that is used to define how information can be shared between systems, government agencies and organizations. Enterprise Architect is integrated with NIEM, and helps you to:
  • Create and develop UML-based Information Exchange Package Documentation (IEPD) models, by providing starter models, model Patterns and a number of toolboxes for creating IEPD models and schema models
  • Generate complete IEPDs from your IEPD model
  • Generate NIEM conformant schemas from your information models
  • Import NIEM Reference Schema into your model
  • Create NIEM subset namespaces, composed from elements of the NIEM Reference Schemas
  • Create PIM, PSM and Model Package Description (MPD) diagrams, using the NIEM Toolbox pages

Enterprise Architect's Schema Composer simplifies the process of creating subset models from the NIEM Reference Models.  The message profile artifact included in the NIEM 4 Starter Model, (also here, at right) allows you to simply double-click the artifact, which opens the Schema Composer, ready for you to start selecting classes for your subset model.

Document Roots

Use this diagram to specify the Root Element of your XML payload document.

The Property 'ExchangeMessage: ExchangeMessageType' is provided as a placeholder that is already linked to the object instance 'NIEM-MPD:ModelPackageDescription'.  You can simply modify the items on this diagram to suit your needs, or add your own items as you see fit.

Technically, the <<qualifiedName>> Usage connector links 'ValidityConstraintWithContext', an instance of the class QualifiedNamesType, to a Document Element that is modeled as a Property within a PropertyHolder.  However, Enterprise Architect has relaxed this requirement and allows you to simply link to the PropertyHolder itself, rather than the Property within.  This also means that you can model the Property as the DestinationRole of an association to the Classifier of the Property.

If the <<qualifiedName>> connector links to the PropertyHolder instead of its Property, the PropertyHolder should contain only one Property.
Package Usage

Use this diagram to show the <<InformationModel>> packages that are linked to the Instance Specification of the ModelPackageDescription.

After creating a NIEM subset model, drop the new <<InformationModel>> packages created by the subsetting process, onto this diagram.

The Usage connectors stereotyped as <<ExtensionSchemaDocument>> and <<SubsetSchemaDocument>>, carry Tagged Values that among other things, are used to record the 'pathURI'.  This specifies the file name and path for the XSD file that will be generated from the linked package when you generate the IEPD.

Enterprise Architect supplies sensible default values for the pathURI, but if you need to change them, place the relevant package on this diagram, select the Usage connector and update the appropriate Tagged Value.

By including artifacts on this diagram and linking them to the ModelPackageDescription instance using appropriately stereotyped Usage connectors, the artifacts will be listed in the file 'mpd-catalog.xml', when the IEPD is generated.

Like the 'Package Usage' diagram, tagged values attached to the Usage connectors are used to specify a number of properties, including the 'pathURI', which represents the filename of the artifact.

Starter Model - NIEM MPD Diagram

The example diagram is part of the NIEM 4 Starter Model, available through the Model Wizard. It provides a convenient starting point for creating your own NIEM 4 model. A user-defined NIEM schema is built around a Model Package Description (MPD). For consumers of the schema, the MPD defines how to use the various XSD files that are included and what message types are being defined. The MPD is created using instances of a number of Classes defined in the UML Profile. Enterprise Architect provides these Classes in a Package that is available through the Model Wizard, or from our Reusable Asset Server. All NIEM 4 models require these MPD types, so that the object instances used to create the MPD can correctly reference the classifiers from which they are derived. The Package 'NIEM MPD Types' is already included in this example model.

The diagram here, illustrates a number of characteristics of a NIEM 4 model, such as:
  • The ModelPackageDescription object instance 'NIEM-MPD'
  • <<InformationModel>> packages
  • The connectors <<ExtensionSchemaDocument>> and <<SubsetSchemaDocument>>
  • Run State values and Tag Values that are specific to NIEM 4,
  • Path URIs are typically specified in the tag values attached to Usage connectors.
It is intended that you begin with the NIEM 4 Starter model, then fill-in or overwrite the Run State variables and tag values of the objects and connectors on the 'MPD Overview' diagram, with values that are appropriate for the model you are creating. Drag new instances of MPD Types onto the diagram as required and use the NIEM 3.0 MPD toolbox to add connectors as necessary. When your model is complete, generate XML Schema Definition files by right-clicking on the Model Package Description object instance, then choose: 'Specialize| NIEM | Generate NIEM Schema'.
NIEM-UML Types for Model Package Description

All NIEM 3 models must be able to reference the Classifier Types defined in this package.  
The NIEM 3 Model Package Description relies on object instances of the Classifiers defined in this package, therefore it is essential that this package is included in any project that seeks to define a NIEM 3 Schema model.

The NIEM 3 MPD Types package is available through the 'New Model from Pattern' wizard.
From the Browser window's header bar menu, select 'New Model from Pattern', choose the NIEM Technology, then select 'NIEM 3 MPD Types'.

elements.name: ModelPackageDescription
elements.notes:
A ModelPackageDescription Artifact represents a NIEM Model Package Description (MPD). Specifically, it represents the information in the NIEM-3 MPD catalog, which is defined for target namespace=http://reference.niem.gov/niem/resource/mpd/catalog/3.0/, in the context of a NIEM-3 subset of the 
niem-core schema.
An MPD is a logical set of electronic files aggregated and organized to fulfill a specific purpose in NIEM. Directory organization and packaging of an MPD should be designed around major themes in NIEM: reuse, sharing, interoperability, and efficiency. The inclusion of artifacts in an MPD is modeled using a Usage dependency from the InstanceSpecification representing the MPD to the model element representing the artifac t (most commonly a Namespace Package). 

The attributes of the ModelPackageDescription correspond to components of the MPDType within the MPD Catalog Schema.  The information model fragment corresponding to c:MPDInformation has been partially flattened from the schema containment structure into the ModelPackageDescription Attributes.   
In addition to the largely isomorphic representation of the MPD Catalog as parts of the ModelPackageDescription, there are a few convenience mechanisms to simplify the UML Mode l.   The representation of the MPD relationship between MPDs is modeled as a «ModelPackageDescriptionRelationship» Dependency from the client ModelPackageDescription Artifact Instance to the related ModelPackageDescription Artifact Instance as supplier.
Instances of ModelPackageDescription may be the client of a UML Usage to some supplying NIEM concept, such as «InformationModel».  These UML Usages may be stereotyped with a sub-stereotype of «FileType».  When such a Usage is defined, values of some stereotype tags may be derived, such as the pathURI (based on UML Package Structure and/or NIEM packaging structure guidelines). Note that most «FileType»s are implicit anyway, being derived by transitive closure of all «InformationModel»s referenced by used «InformationModel»s.

Schema Composer

The Schema Composer can be accessed from the 'Design' ribbon, by selecting the option:  'Tools > Schema Composer', or
double-click an existing Schema Profile artifact, to open that schema profile in the Schema Composer.

The Schema Composer is a versatile tool for quickly and easily defining a variety of formal schema from a model. Many industries have worked hard to define shared meta-models specific to their industry. These models now form the basis for contractual information sharing amongst organizations within those industries. When information is shared between organizations, it is often the case that only a subset of the full meta-model is required. In this case, the Schema Composer is the perfect tool for deriving contractual schema based on subsets and restricted data sets taken from the meta-model as a whole. So, a typical usage scenario of the Schema Composer, is in the creation of message definitions (schema) to exchange information between organizations, ensuring that such messages comply with meta-model definitions, adopted for use by those organizations. The Schema Composer avoids the common 'pain points' of working with XSD and other schema languages directly:
  • There is no need to create a relatively complex XSD model composed of specific XSD elements in addition to your 'normal' business and data models, to define the required data, its associations and references, and any restrictions or conditions
  • You do not need to understand how to use the XSD elements and apply the XSD naming rules and conventions to correctly construct such models; formatting and naming rules as specified by the supported standards are automatically applied during generation of the schema.
The Schema Composer greatly simplifies the process of creating standards compliant schema in a re-usable and accessible manner.
See also:

When any named XML or JSON schema facet exists in the Tagged Value domain of an attribute the Schema Composer emits the appropriate restrictions.

Example: The postcode attribute of Address has a length constraint that can be seen in the tagged value list when the attribute is selected.

A Deployment diagram shows how and where a system is to be deployed; that is, its execution architecture.
Hardware devices, processors and software execution environments (system Artifacts) are reflected as Nodes, and the internal construction can be depicted by embedding or nesting Nodes. 
Deployment relationships indicate the deployment of Artifacts, and Manifest relationships reveal the physical implementation of Components. As Artifacts are allocated to Nodes to model the system's deployment, the allocation is guided by the use of Deployment Specifications.

A Deployment diagram's elements and connectors are created from the Deployment pages of the diagram toolbox.

elements.name: Add2
elements.notes:
Constraint Block: Add2 Adds the two inputs together, placing the resultant number in output. Algebraically, the function can be expressed as such: output = a + b Where:
  • a: The first number to add
  • b: The second number to add

elements.name: Add3
elements.notes:
Constraint Block: Add3 Adds the three inputs together, placing the resultant number in output. Algebraically, the function can be expressed as such: output = a + b + c Where:
  • a: The first number to add
  • b: The second number to add
  • c: The third number to add

elements.name: Delay
elements.notes:
Constraint Block: Delay Offsets the original signal, input, by delay timesteps and outputs the resultant signal to output. Algebraically, the function can be expressed as such: outputt = inputt - delay Where:
  • input: The input signal
  • t: The current time
  • delay: The number of timesteps in the past to offset the input signal by.
Note: See individual parameter notes for more information.

elements.notes: EchoDSP - Parametric diagram

elements.name: Mult
elements.notes:
Constraint Block: Mult Outputs the value of a, scaled by a factor of b using the formula: output = a * b Where:
  • a: Input value
  • b: Scaling factor
Note: See individual parameter notes for more information.

elements.name: SineWave
elements.notes:
Constraint Block: SineWave Generates a sine wave according to the function: output = a * sin( f * 2π * t ) Where:
  • a: Amplitude
  • f: Frequency
  • t: Time
Note: See individual parameter notes for more information.

This parametric diagram describes the 'Echo' audio effect used by the DSP.
  1. The original sound source is created by the Constraint Block instance of :SineWave.
  2. The echo signal is then generated by scaling the original signal through :Mult and offsetting it by a prescribed amount of time steps in :Delay.

  • amplitude: 5 (eg 5 decibels)
  • f: 0.5 (eg 2 cycles per second = 2 hertz)
  • t: 0 - 10 [0.05] (eg Simulate from 0 - 10 seconds calculating every 0.05 seconds)
  • att: 0.5 (eg echo signal will be half of the volume of the original signal)
  • offset: 1 (eg use the original signal value from 1 timestep ago to calculate the echo signal).

The Test Case element is a stereotyped Use Case element.
It is available through the Use Case and Maintenance pages of the Toolbox.
Test Case elements allow you to define the details of tests that apply to each of several elements, instead of recording the details separately in each element.  Within the Test Case element's properties, you can define test requirements and constraints.  You can also associate the test with test files, link the element to Document Artifacts or directly to Linked Documents, such as a Test Plan.
The Test Case element enables you to give greater visibility to tests, in the Browser window, Diagram List, Package Browser, Model Search, Relationship Matrix, Traceability Window and reports.

Use Case Diagram

Use Case diagrams can be created with the system represented by a Boundary that contains the Use Cases.  

Enterprise Architect provides a sophisticated editor where modelers can specify the steps that make up scenarios, including any constraints that may apply.  

Behavior diagrams can be generated from the scenarios, allowing the steps to be visualized.
Tracing Requirements
Scenario Builder

The Responsibility window provides a convenient means for quickly viewing, adding and editing rules that apply to an element. To show the Responsibility window, from the 'Design' ribbon, select the option: 'Element > Requirements > Scenarios' The window shows details of the entities that impose such rules or restrictions on the element, namely:
  • The element's scenarios
  • The element's internal constraints (not external Constraint notes)
  • The element's internal responsibilities or requirements
The detailed steps of a Use Case can be recorded and linked to other elements in the model. A number of different diagrams can be automatically generated from the Use Case steps and Scenarios. The diagram and the text can be synchronized and individual steps can then be traced to other elements such as Components that will realize the Requirement specified in the Use Case.

Class diagrams are one of the most ubiquitous of the UML diagrams and can be used to model structural and semantic relationship from business domain models to models of programming source code.

A Component diagram illustrates the pieces of software, embedded controllers and such that make up a system, and their organization and dependencies.
A Component diagram has a higher level of abstraction than a Class diagram; usually a component is implemented by one or more Classes (or Objects) at runtime. They are building blocks, built up so that eventually a component can encompass a large portion of a system.

'Navigation Options' allow you to specify, within the Element Browser, node types to show or hide. As of EA 15, the Navigation Options can now be saved as named sets, allowing you to switch easily from one set to another. To see an example, perform these steps:
  1. Select 'Class1' in the diagram.
  2. Display the Element Browser.
  3. Right-click in the Element Browser, then choose 'Navigation Options'.
  4. In the 'Select Visible' dialog, select 'Operations', 'Attributes' and 'Receptions' and deselect all others.
  5. Save this selection as 'Atts and Ops'.
  6. Now select 'Requirements', 'Constraints' and 'Scenarios' and deselect all others.
  7. Save this selection as 'Reqs'.
  8. Click on the OK button to dismiss the 'Select Visible' dialog.
You can now right-click in the Element Browser and select 'Atts and Ops' to show only the nodes from that set, or choose 'Reqs' to show only the nodes in that set.
Element - Info View

The elements on this diagram have had features added to them, to provide examples of each of the different types of element compartment that can be displayed. Visibility of the element compartments can be set at the diagram level, as well as visibility of additional compartments being set for individual elements on the diagram. To set diagram level compartment visibility: Double-click on the background of the diagram to open the diagram's Properties dialog, then select the 'Elements' page. At the center of this page is a large checklist that allows you to enable and disable the display of each compartment. This affects all elements on the diagram. To enable compartment visibility for an individual element: Right-click on a diagram element, then choose 'Compartment Visibility' from the pop-up menu. In the 'Select Visibility' dialog, select any additional compartments that you want to display for this element. Note: Selecting a compartment in this checklist will show that compartment for this element, however, deselecting compartments here will not hide a compartment that is made visible at the diagram level.

As of EA 15.2, the Element Browser has become the 'Details' tab of the Inspector window. When used in conjunction with the docked Properties window, the 'Details' tab provides quick and easy access to the details of any and all of an element's properties. As an example, run through these steps:
  • Ensure that the docked Properties window is showing (ribbon: 'Start > All Windows > Design > Explore > Properties')
  • Ensure that the 'Details' tab is showing (ribbon: 'Start > All Windows > Design > Explore > Inspect > Details')
  • On the diagram, select 'Class1'

  • Click within the 'Details' tab, then press (Ctrl '+ ') to expand all nodes
  • Click on the various nodes within the 'Details' tab and observe that the details for the selected item are displayed in the docked Properties window
  • Select a different element on the diagram; the contents of the 'Details' tab are updated accordingly, allowing you to inspect properties of this element's features

In Enterprise Architect 15, the handling of tagged values in the user interface has changed.

Prior to EA 15, stereotype properties for elements were available on a separate page of the properties window, along with the tagged values window. Connectors, attributes and operations did not have this functionality. In EA 15, they are now displayed in the property list, alongside the properties for the UML base class being extended. These are usually of equal or greater importance to modeling in those languages.

Prior to EA 15, tagged values not coming from a profile were available in the tagged values window. This resulted in another window that you were effectively forced to show, even if they were rarely used. In EA 15, these tagged values are available on a separate page of the properties window.

This first example shows two similar requirements. The first is a SysML 1.5 Functional requirement. If SysML 1.5 is available, the stereotype properties will display in the main property list. This example demonstrates how to Record Program Execution and create Test Sets, using Enterprise Architect's Execution Recorder.
Guide:

This example makes use of sample source code that is part of your Enterprise Architect installation.
The sample code for this example is installed to:  "C:\Program Files (x86)\Sparx Systems\EA\Code Samples\VEA"
but should be copied to a different location, so that you don't need to run with elevated permissions in order to compile and build the project.
So, for example, copy everything in "C:\Program Files (x86)\Sparx Systems\EA\Code Samples\VEA", 
to "C:\EA_CodeSamples\VEA".

Before running the example, you must configure Local Path definitions for %VEA% and %MSVS%.
-    %VEA% = "C:\EA_CodeSamples\VEA"    (the directory into which you copied the sample code)
-    %MSVS% = "C:\program files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio 9.0\Common7\IDE"
(From the 'Develop' ribbon, select the option 'Source Code > Options > Configure Local Paths'.)

1.  Open the Record and Analyze window.  It can be accessed from the 'Execute' ribbon, by selecting the option 'Tools > Recorder > Open Recorder'.
2.  Open the Execution Analyzer window.  It can be accessed from the 'Execute' ribbon, by selecting the option 'Tools > Analyzer'.
3.  Locate the Analyzer script 'Book Test'.  It can be found in the Execution Analyzer window under 'Visual Execution Analysis..Net.Source'.
4.  Select the script (by placing a checkmark), then build the project by clicking the 'Build' button.
5.  View the source code for class Test.  Select class Test on this diagram, then right-click and choose 'Code Engineering > View Source Code'.
6.  Place a recording marker at the instantiation of BookDB in the function RunBookStore() - on line 123.  Create a breakpoint on this line, then open its Properties and set the action to 'Start Recording'.
7.   Run the program.
8.  The program execution is recorded from the point where execution hits the recording marker. The Record and Analyze window displays the results of the recording.
9.  Use the drop-down arrow attached to the left-most toolbar button on the Record and Analyze window to show its command menu.  This menu includes options to generate a range of diagrams from the information recorded during program execution.
10.  Generate all diagrams.

These images show examples of the Testpoints window, the Testpoint editor and sample trace output in the System Output window.
This example demonstrates how to create and use Testpoints, to verify your application.

This example makes use of output produced by the 'Recording Execution' example. Before running this example, please run through the 'Recording Execution' example and generate all of the diagrams, as outlined in step 10.
  1. The example 'Recording Execution' produces a number of diagrams, each one named 'BookTestClient_Test_RunBookStore'. One of these diagrams is a 'Test Domain' diagram - open the Test Domain diagram. It should contain one <<testset>> element and four <<testcut>> elements.
  2. Open the Testpoints window. It can be accessed from the 'Execute' ribbon, by selecting the option 'Analyze > Testing > Show Testpoints Window'.
  3. With the Testpoints window showing, select in turn each of the various elements on the Test Domain diagram. Notice that the contents of the Testpoints window update to show different Classes, operations and constraints, depending on which <<testcut>> or <<testset>> element is selected on the diagram.
  4. Select the <<testset>> element 'BookTestClient_Test_RunBookStore' on the diagram, then click the Run Tests button on the toolbar of the Testpoints window. The tests are evaluated as the program runs and the test results are tabulated in the Testpoints window.
  5. In the Testpoints window, select the operation PriceTotaller.AveragePrice(), then right-click and choose 'Add Testpoint'.
  6. In the Testpoint editor window, choose 'Pre-Condition' as the type, specify the 'Condition' as 'countBooks = 0', and set 'Action on Fail' to 'Continue'. Add a Trace Statement as shown: Demonstration -- countBooks = @countBooks - anything non-ZERO is actually OK! (Note: For demonstration purposes, we are deliberately setting a condition that should always fail, namely 'countBooks = 0'. Under normal circumstances we would specify a condition that we want to evaluate as 'True', such as 'countBooks > 0'.)
  7. Click on the OK button to save the changes.
  8. Click on 'Run Tests'. The Testpoints window updates to show the test results. You should see that the new test has been executed one time, and it failed.
  9. Open the System Output window and select the 'Testpoints' page. You should see the trace output from the Pre-Condition test that was added to AveragePrice().
